Fast and Stable Arbitrary Precision Approximate Matrix Multiplication

**Abstract**

We present several new and surprising results on the theory and practice of Arbitrary Precision Approximate (APA) matrix multiplication, which refers to algorithms that output merely approximations to matrix multiplication even in exact arithmetic. While APA algorithms have been around for nearly half a century, and despite the fact that they have potentially lower (asymptotic) cost than many fast exact matrix multiplication schemes, they have not been studied as closely, to the extent that relatively little is known about their numerical properties. In this paper, we shine a spotlight on these algorithms by presenting three important results. First, we provide a new search algorithm for APA routines that is easy to use, automatically generates encoding matrices with functional entries, and can match or beat the best known APA algorithms for several sizes. In particular, we improve the upper bound on the border rank of \(\langle 2,4,5\rangle\) matrix multiplication. Second, we combine this insight with alternative bases to minimize the number of additions in an APA algorithm, thereby improving its leading coefficient. Finally, we prove the same kind of stability that characterizes fast exact matrix multiplication for an algorithm of Bini [_Calcolo_ 1980] that computes an exact product of two matrices using a modified APA scheme (with or without alternative bases).

**Keywords:** Matrix multiplication, arbitrary precision, border rank, alternative bases, floating-point stability

**MSC Class:** 65F99

## 1 Introduction

In 1969, Strassen [59] fundamentally changed the field of numerical linear algebra when he demonstrated that the classical algorithm for matrix multiplication is not optimal. Strassen’s discovery sparked a still ongoing effort to derive, analyze, and implement _fast_ matrix multiplication algorithms, which are broadly defined as any matrix multiplication routine with computational complexity \(O(n^\omega)\) for \(2\le\omega<3\). At the time of writing, Dupont et al. [27] hold the record for the smallest value of \(\omega\) achieved by an algorithm, and it remains open whether the lower bound \(\omega\ge 2\) is attainable. Research aimed at reaching this lower bound (or proving it cannot be done) is motivated by both the wide applicability of matrix multiplication in scientific computing/machine learning and the fact that many linear algebra operations have been shown to reduce to matrix multiplication [20], including recently nonsymmetric eigenvalue problems [5, 22].

Most practical fast matrix multiplication algorithms, including Strassen’s [59], are based on routines for multiplying small matrices. The key idea here is straightforward: an algorithm for multiplying \(m_0\times k_0\) and \(k_0\times n_0\) matrices can be used to compute the product of arbitrary \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\) and \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) by breaking the input into blocks

\(A=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c } A_{11} & \cdots & A_{1k_0} \\ \vdots &  & \vdots \\ A_{m_01} & \cdots & A_{m_0k_0} \end{array}\right)B=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c } B_{11} & \cdots & B_{1n_0} \\ \vdots &  & \vdots \\ B_{k_01} & \cdots & B_{k_0n_0} \end{array}\right)\) (1.1)

and applying the algorithm at the block level. In this context, each scalar multiplication in the original "base-case" algorithm becomes a matrix multiplication of size \((m/m_0)\times(k/k_0)\) by \((k/k_0)\times(n/n_0)\), assuming for simplicity that _m_<sub>0</sub>, _k_<sub>0</sub>, and _n_<sub>0</sub> divide _m_, _k_, and _n_, respectively. This procedure can then be used to handle the smaller block multiplications, continuing recursively either until the base case \(m_0\times k_0\) by \(k_0\times n_0\) is reached or, more commonly, until the block size is small enough to handle with classical matrix multiplication. The result is a (general) matrix multiplication algorithm of complexity _O_((_mkn_)<sup>log<sub>_m_<sub>0</sub>_k_<sub>0</sub>_n_<sub>0</sub></sup>(_t_)</sup>), where _t_ is the number of scalar multiplications in the base-case routine. When _m=n=k_, this simplifies to \(O(n^\omega)\) for \(\omega=3log_{m_0k_0n_0}(t)\). Throughout, we use \(\langle m,k,n\rangle\) and \(\langle m,k,n;t\rangle\) to refer, respectively, to \(m\times k\) by \(k\times n\) matrix multiplication and an algorithm for it that uses _t_ scalar multiplications.

The above observations underpin one branch of research on fast matrix multiplication, which is focused on searching for optimal routines for small matrices \[3,24,28,39,41,44,47,49,50,55,56\], where "optimality" is measured by the number of scalar multiplications used. Algorithms derived this way are sometimes referred to as _feasible_ fast matrix multiplication because, while they typically do not achieve the best known upper bounds on \(\omega\), they are applicable to inputs of more manageable size, making them candidates for practical use.<sup>1</sup> Accordingly, significant effort has been placed on optimizing these routines beyond their asymptotic complexity (see \[32\]).

The search for small matrix multiplication routines led to the discovery of Arbitrary Precision Approximate or APA matrix multiplication algorithms in the late 70’s. First coined by Bini et al. \[10\], APA matrix multiplication refers to a class of bilinear algorithms that, given input matrices _A_ and _B_ and an evaluation parameter \(\varepsilon\), computes

\(AB+\varepsilon R_1+\varepsilon^2R_2+\cdots+\varepsilon^dR_d,\) (1.2)

where _R_<sub>1</sub>_,...,R<sub>d</sub>_ are residual matrices (that depend on _A_ and _B_) and _d_ is the _degree_ of the algorithm. Note that the approximation obtained from an APA routine can be made arbitrarily accurate by taking \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\). An example of an APA algorithm for multiplying \(3\times 2\) and \(2\times 2\) matrices - alongside both classical and fast exact alternatives - is shown in Figure 1, which in particular emphasizes how each algorithm obtains its output (exact or approximate) from a certain number of scalar multiplications.

From Figure 1 we see that APA matrix multiplication can (at least in some cases) be accomplished with fewer scalar products than exact matrix multiplication. In fact, Hopcroft and Kerr \[34\] showed that computing the exact product of a \(3\times 2\) and \(2\times 2\) matrix requires at least 11 scalar multiplications and hence that no exact algorithm is capable of beating the 10 multiplication APA routine of Bini et al. \[10\]. One way to understand this is through the lens of tensor decomposition; exact and APA algorithms for \(m\times k\) by \(k\times n\) matrix multiplication can be interpreted as exact and approximate decompositions of the \(\langle m,k,n\rangle\) matrix multiplication tensor, which is defined as

\(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}:=\sum_{i_1=1}^m\sum_{i_2=1}^k\sum_{i_3=1}^nE_{i_1i_2}^{(m,k)}\otimes E_{i_2i_3}^{(k,n)}\otimes E_{i_3i_1}^{(n,m)}.\) (1.3)

Here, \(\otimes\) is the Kronecker product and \(E_{ij}^{(m,n)}\) is an \(m\times n\) standard basis matrix, whose only nonzero entry is a one in row _i_ and column _j_.<sup>2</sup> Each scalar multiplication in an exact/APA algorithm contributes a rank-one tensor (e.g., one term in the sum (1.3)) to the corresponding decomposition of \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\). Accordingly, the number of scalar multiplications in an exact algorithm provides an upper bound on the _rank_ of \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\), that is, the minimum number of rank-one tensors needed to construct \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\). The same can be said of an APA algorithm and the _border_ rank of \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\), which corresponds to the minimum number of rank-one tensors in a sequence of decompositions whose limit is \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\). In this language, the above example can be summarized as follows: the rank and border rank of \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle 3,2,2\rangle}\) are 11 and 10 respectively,<sup>3</sup> and corresponding decompositions can be obtained from the algorithms in Figure 1. For more background on tensor (border) rank and the notation used here, see \[42\] and \[8, Section 2\].

Despite this, APA algorithms are typically not used in practice. One reason is apparent from Figure 1: APA matrix multiplication requires dividing by \(\varepsilon\), which means we cannot hope to use it in the limit \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\) to obtain the exact product _C=AB_ (at least in the presence of floating-point roundoff).

In the recursive setting, (1.4) implies that the number of evaluations necessary to obtain the exact product of arbitrary \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\) and \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) has logarithmic dependence on the size of the matrices.<sup>4</sup> That is, the complexity of an APA matrix multiplication algorithm is \(O(L\cdot(mkn)^{log_{m_0k_0n_0}(t)})\), where _L_ must satisfy (1.4) with equality to get the improved exponent.

The extra logarithmic factor here implies that, while the exponent \(\omega=log_{m_0k_0n_0}(t)\) may be lower than what can be achieved by fast exact \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0\rangle\) matrix multiplication, APA algorithms, evaluated enough times to get an exact output, can only offer practical speedups on (possibly galactically) large matrices. For this reason, they have historically been considered mainly of theoretical interest, primarily as a source of upper bounds on the border rank of \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\). This is no doubt compounded by the fact that techniques for deriving APA algorithms are poorly documented in the literature. The most popular search algorithm applies some version of (nonlinear or alternating) least squares to the tensor decomposition problem. While least squares is similarly used to find fast exact algorithms (see e.g., \[3, 56\]), this approach has a unique limitation in the APA setting: the need to convert numerical decompositions into ones with functional entries. There is no known algorithmic way to do this. Indeed, Smirnov uses "various choice heuristics" to obtain many of the current best-known APA algorithms in \[56\]. Other open questions concern the practical details of using APA matrix multiplication. For example, recalling that fast exact matrix multiplication is well-known to be (norm-wise) stable \[20\], can the same be said of the "exactification" procedure introduced by Bini \[9\]? Additionally, can we accelerate an APA algorithm using the same tools applied to fast exact matrix multiplication, specifically the alternative basis approach of Holtz et al. \[32\]?

The goal of this work is to address all three of these questions. Our first contribution is a new search algorithm for APA matrix multiplication routines that can be easily run on small values of _m_<sub>0</sub>, _k_<sub>0</sub>, and _n_<sub>0</sub>, requires minimal computing resources, and automatically generates decompositions with functional entries (e.g., of the form shown in Figure 2). Alongside this search algorithm, we also extend both the aforementioned numerical stability results and the alternative basis procedure to the APA setting. One strong motivation for this work is the rapidly changing (and varied) set of demands placed on matrix multiplication kernels by machine learning applications (see the discussion in \[23\]), which warrants revisiting every option in our algorithmic toolkit. Note in particular that an APA algorithm may only be slower than fast exact matrix multiplication in practice if we evaluate it enough times to get an exact product; in applications where only a low-precision approximate product is necessary - and hence evaluating an APA algorithm _O_(1) may be sufficient - APA matrix multiplication will be competitive. Indeed, Ballard et al. \[4\] have already obtained promising results in this direction in the context of neural network training.

## 1.1 Our Contributions

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

1. In Section 2 we present a new algorithm for generating APA matrix multiplication routines. The key insight is the following: by applying a symbolic De-Groote transformation and deleting one rank-one term in the corresponding tensor decomposition, a fast exact algorithm yields an APA routine with one fewer scalar multiplication (assuming the product of the factors in the deleted term is nilpotent). Using the recently introduced flip graph \[39, 50\] to find exact algorithms where this condition is satisfied, we obtain new APA routines for a variety of matrix sizes, including one that improves the previously best-known rank.<tbc>

<sup>4</sup>Note that making the base case routine exact via (1.6) and using that recursively would lead to a slower algorithm.

2. In Section 3, we extend the alternative basis work of \[32, 38\] to APA matrix multiplication. In doing so, we demonstrate that fast, symbolic basis transformations can be used to "sparsify" APA algorithms and therefore improve the leading coefficient in their arithmetic complexities.<tbc>

3. In Section 4, we show that the approximate-to-exact procedure of Bini \[9\] is stable (under some mild assumptions). In particular, we prove a weak forward stability bound for this procedure, in floating- point arithmetic and including the fast basis transformations from Section 3, that matches the format of existing bounds for fast exact matrix multiplication \[21, 53\]. To our knowledge, these are the first stability bounds of any kind for APA matrix multiplication. We also comment on the stability of evaluating an APA algorithm a fixed number of times.<tbc>

4. Finally, Section 5 presents a handful of numerical examples that validate the theoretical results from the previous sections.

Our results are captured by s 1 and 2, which show, respectively, the best ranks achieved in our search (vs. existing results in the literature) and improvements to the leading coefficient of APA algorithms obtained by sparsifying with alternative bases.

## 1.2 Notation and Conventions

In the remainder of the paper, the matrices _A_, _B_, and their product _C=AB_ are assumed to be complex. As mentioned above, we use \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0\rangle\) to refer to \(m_0\times k_0\) by \(k_0\times n_0\) matrix multiplication (either exact or approximate) and \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0;t\rangle\) to refer to algorithms for this problem that use _t_ scalar multiplications. Note that \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0\rangle\) is equivalent to \(\langle m_0,n_0,k_0\rangle\), \(\langle k_0,m_0,n_0\rangle\), \(\langle k_0,n_0,m_0\rangle\), \(\langle n_0,m_0,k_0\rangle\), and \(\langle n_0,k_0,m_0\rangle\) in the sense that an algorithm for one can be adapted to an algorithm for any of the others (with the same number of scalar multiplications but possibly different additive complexity) \[33\].

Note that the potential practical efficiency of an \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0;t\rangle\) matrix multiplication algorithm can be gleaned from properties of its encoding matrices. For example, a _real_ algorithm, whose encoding matrices are all real valued, in practice, is likely faster than a _complex_ one (of comparable sparsity), which requires complex arithmetic even to multiply real matrices. Similarly, an algorithm with sparse encoding matrices will likely be faster in practice - hence the reference above to "sparsifying" an APA algorithm, which really refers to sparsifying its encoding matrices (see \[7\]).

Throughout, we use \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)\), \(\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\) and \(\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]\), to denote, respectively, the field of rational functions, the ring of polynomials, and the ring of Laurent polynomials in the variable \(\varepsilon\) with complex coefficients. We also use Matlab notation when convenient, e.g., _A_(:_,i_) and _A(i,_:) refer to a column/row of the matrix _A_. This extends to arbitrary index sets _I_. That is, _A_(:_,I_) collects the columns of _A_ with indices \(i\in I\).

**Remark 1.1.** In this paper, we assume that the remainder of an APA algorithm, meaning the difference between its output and the true product, takes the form \(\varepsilon R_1+\cdots+\varepsilon^dR_d\), where _R<sub>i</sub>_ is assumed to be not identically zero for all \(1\le i\le d\). This does not necessarily hold for all APA algorithms, which may have remainders that skip terms (see  1). This is relevant for implementation purposes since, in practice, the number of evaluations necessary to recover the exact product _AB_ from an APA algorithm is not determined by the largest exponent in its remainder but rather by the number of nonzero terms it contains. The catch here is that the number of terms in the remainder for a recursive implementation of a \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0\rangle\) APA algorithm (that performs _L_ recursive steps) is _not_ necessarily _L_ times the number of terms in the base- case algorithm, and in fact in most cases it grows to _dL_ as _L_ increases. For this reason we stick with \(\varepsilon R_1+\cdots+\varepsilon^dR_d\) in our analysis.

## 2 A New Search Algorithm for APA Schemes

We start by presenting a new algorithm for deriving APA schemes. As mentioned above, existing methods for generating APA algorithms, e.g., those of Smirnov and Bini, take (approximate) floating-point decompositions of the matrix multiplication tensor and convert them into symbolic ones. Our approach flips this idea; we start from an exact algorithm and produce an APA one by applying a symbolic De-Groote transformation and subsequently deleting terms that are \(O(\varepsilon)\). That is, if \(\sum_{j=1}^rU_j\otimes V_j\otimes W_j\) is a decomposition of the matrix multiplication tensor \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\) for \(U_j\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\), \(V_j\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) and \(W_j\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}\) (recall Figure 2), then

\(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}=\sum_{j=1}^rR^{-1}U_jS\otimes S^{-1}V_jT\otimes T^{-1}W_jR\) (2.1)

for any invertible _R_, _S_, and _T_. If additionally _R_, _S_, and _T_ have entries in \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)\), we obtain a symbolic decomposition that is exact for any value of \(\varepsilon\). Deleting the terms for which every nonzero entry of \(R^{-1}U_jS\otimes S^{-1}V_jT\otimes T^{-1}W_jR\) is divisible by a positive power of \(\varepsilon\) yields an APA algorithm (possibly of lower rank) that can be made arbitrarily accurate as \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\).

The difficulty of this approach lies in finding an appropriate exact algorithm to use as a starting point (as we will see, not just any one will do). One way of doing this is by using recent work on generating exact decompositions \[39, 50\], which allows us to find exact algorithms satisfying the necessary conditions to produce lower rank APA algorithms. In this section, we provide an overview of this approach, including pseudocode and a motivating example, and discuss the results of our search.

## 2.1 Sufficient Conditions for Rank Improvements

Suppose that an exact algorithm for matrix multiplication is represented by the tensor decomposition \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}=\sum_{j=1}^rU_j\otimes V_j\otimes W_j\). This algorithm is a good starting point for the approach outlined above if the following hold: (1) the product _U<sub>j</sub>V<sub>j</sub>W<sub>j</sub>_ is nilpotent for at least one _j_ (required) and (2) _r_ is small (desired but not required). The second criterion is one of practical concern; since we obtain APA algorithms by removing terms from an exact one, we stand to obtain the best result by starting from an exact algorithm that has minimal rank. The first criterion, on the other hand, guarantees that a term can be deleted at all. We verify this below.

**Theorem 2.1.** _Suppose that the product UVW of_ \(U\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\), \(V\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) _and_ \(W\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m}\) _is nilpotent. In this case, there exist_ \(R\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{m\times m}\), \(S\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{k\times k}\)_, and_ \(T\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{n\times n}\)_, each invertible over_ \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)\)_, such that all entries of R_<sup>-1</sup>_US, S_<sup>-1</sup>_VT, and T_<sup>-1</sup>_WR are polynomials in_ \(\varepsilon\) _with zero constant term._

_Proof._ Let _F_<sub>0</sub>=_G_<sub>0</sub>=_H_<sub>0</sub>=0 and inductively define _F_<sub>_j_+1</sub>, _G_<sub>_j_+1</sub>, and _H_<sub>_j_+1</sub> to be the pre-images of _G<sub>j</sub>_, _H<sub>j</sub>_, and _F<sub>j</sub>_, respectively, under the linear transformations represented by _W_, _V_, and _U_. For example, _F_<sub>1</sub>=ker(_W_), _G_<sub>1</sub>=ker(_V_), and _H_<sub>1</sub>=ker(_U_). We note two important facts about these subspaces:

1. They are nested - e.g., \(F_j\subseteq F_{j+1}\), \(G_j\subseteq G_{j+1}\), and \(H_j\subseteq H_{j+1}\). This can be shown inductively by first noting that \(F_0\subseteq F_1\) (since \(x\in F_0\) satisfies \(Wx=W0=0\in G_0\)), \(G_0\subseteq G_1\), and \(H_0\subseteq H_1\). Now, \(F_j\subseteq F_{j+1}\) implies \(H_{j+1}\subseteq H_{j+2}\), \(G_j\subseteq G_{j+1}\Rightarrow F_{j+1}\subseteq F_{j+2}\), and \(H_j\subseteq H_{j+1}\Rightarrow G_{j+1}\subseteq G_{j+2}\).<tbc>

2. _F_<sub>3_i_</sub>, _G_<sub>3_i_</sub>, and _H_<sub>3_i_</sub> are the null spaces of (_UVW)<sup>i</sup>_, (_WUV)<sup>i</sup>_, and (_VWU)<sup>i</sup>_, respectively.

If _UVW_ is nilpotent, then so are _VWU_ and _WUV_,<sup>6</sup> and therefore \(\bigcup_jF_j=\mathbb{C}^m\), \(\bigcup_jG_j=\mathbb{C}^n\), and \(\bigcup_jH_j=\mathbb{C}^k\). Define _S_ and _T_ analogously using _H<sub>j</sub>_ and _G<sub>j</sub>_. It remains to show that _R_<sup>-1</sup>_US_, _S_<sup>-1</sup>_VT_, and _T_<sup>-1</sup>_WR_ have entries in \(\varepsilon\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\). By construction, we have \(R^{-1}USy=\varepsilon^iR^{-1}Uy\) and moreover \(Uy\in F_{i-1}\), so \(Uy=\alpha_1x_1+\cdots+\alpha_lx_l\) for the basis vectors _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>l</sub>_ of C_<sup>m</sup>_ coming from _F_<sub>_i_-1</sub>. But in this case,

\(R^{-1}USy=\varepsilon^iR^{-1}\left(\alpha_1x_1+\cdots+\alpha_lx_l\right)=\varepsilon^i\left(\alpha_1R^{-1}x_1+\cdots+\alpha_lR^{-1}x_l\right)=\alpha_1\varepsilon^{i-\beta_1}x_1+\cdots+\alpha_l\varepsilon^{i-\beta_l}x_l,\) (2.2)

Since this applies to any basis vector \(y\in\mathbb{C}^k\), and letting \(Y\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times k}\) be the matrix containing that basis, we conclude that _R_<sup>-1</sup>_USY_ has entries in \(\varepsilon\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\), which is sufficient to show the same for the entries of _R_<sup>-1</sup>_US_, since multiplying on the right by _Y_ <sup>-1</sup>, which has constant entries, won’t introduce any constant terms. The same argument can be used to show that _S_<sup>-1</sup>_VT_ and _T_<sup>-1</sup>_WR_ also have entries in \(\varepsilon\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\).

The key idea behind our search algorithm is now captured by the following result. The terms corresponding to \(j\le l\), which can be transformed to have entries that are polynomials in \(\varepsilon\) with no constant term - a property that carries over to the corresponding tensor product \(R^{-1}U_jS\otimes S^{-1}V_jT\otimes T^{-1}W_jR\) - are precisely those we referred to as \(O(\varepsilon)\) above.

**Theorem 2.2.** _Let_ \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}=\sum_{j=1}^rU_j\otimes V_j\otimes W_j\) _be a tensor decomposition obtained from an exact_ \(\langle m,k,n\rangle\) _matrix multiplication algorithm. If there exist_ \(R\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{m\times m}\), \(S\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{k\times k}\)_, and_ \(T\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{n\times n}\)_, each invertible over_ \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)\)_, such that R_<sup>-1</sup>_U<sub>j</sub>S, S_<sup>-1</sup>_V<sub>j</sub>T, and T_<sup>-1</sup>_W<sub>j</sub>R have entries in_ \(\varepsilon\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\) _for all_ \(1\le j\le l\)_, then_

\(\sum_{j=l+1}^rR^{-1}U_jS\otimes S^{-1}V_jT\otimes T^{-1}W_jR\)

_is an approximate, symbolic decomposition of_ \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\) _that corresponds to an APA algorithm of rank r-l. In particular, the border rank of_ \(\mathcal{M}_{\langle m,k,n\rangle}\) _is bounded by r-l._

Theorem 2.2 implies that we can remove more than one nilpotent term from an exact decomposition provided they can be made \(O(\varepsilon)\) for the same (symbolic) basis transformations. Despite this, Theorem 2.1 only provides a criterion for removing one term at a time, which is ultimately limited by the fact that, even if we have two terms that correspond to nilpotent products, a set of transformations that makes one \(O(\varepsilon)\) may not necessarily make the other \(O(\varepsilon)\) as well. Hence, we need other tools for identifying when more than one term is removable The following proposition gives an easy necessary condition.

**Proposition 2.3.** _If R_<sup>-1</sup>_U<sub>j</sub>S, S_<sup>-1</sup>_V<sub>j</sub>T, and T_<sup>-1</sup>_W<sub>j</sub>R have entries in_ \(\varepsilon\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\) _for all_ \(1\le j\le l\) _and R, S, and T as in Theorem 2.2, then_

\(\mathrm{Trace}(U_{j_1^u}V_{j_1^v}W_{j_1^w}\cdots U_{j_p^u}V_{j_p^v}W_{j_p^w})=0\)

_for all sequences of indices_ \(j_1^u,j_1^v,j_1^w,\dots,j_p^u,j_p^v,j_p^w\le l\) _with_ \(p\ge 1\).

_Proof._ Since trace is basis invariant, all expressions of the form \(\mathrm{Trace}(U_{j_1^u}V_{j_1^v}W_{j_1^w}\dots U_{j_p^u}V_{j_p^v}W_{j_p^w})\) are invariant under De-Groote transformations. By assumption, we have a De-Groote transformation under which the given expression is a polynomial in \(\varepsilon\) with zero constant term. But the original expression does not depend on \(\varepsilon\), so it follows that it must be zero.

Importantly, this necessary condition is also a sufficient one. Moreover, we do not need to check arbitrary products of the _U<sub>j</sub>V<sub>j</sub>W<sub>j</sub>_ (which of course is not possible in practice). This follows from classical results in invariant theory, namely Hilbert’s basis theorem and Hilbert-Mumford, though an effective bound for _p_ is given by Le Bruyn and Procesi \[45, Theorem 1\]. In the literature, this theorem is usually stated in the language of quivers, which we reformulate in our context.<sup>7</sup>

**Theorem 2.4.** _Suppose that_ \(\mathrm{Trace}(U_{j_1^u}V_{j_1^v}W_{j_1^w}\cdots U_{j_p^u}V_{j_p^v}W_{j_p^w})=0\) _for all sequences of indices_ \(j_1^u,j_1^v,j_1^w,\dots\dots,j_p^u,j_p^v,j_p^w\le l\) _with_ \(p\le(m+k+n)^2\)_. Then there exist_ \(R\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{m\times m}\), \(S\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{k\times k}\)_, and_ \(T\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{n\times n}\)_, each invertible over_ \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)\)_, such that R_<sup>-1</sup>_U<sub>j</sub>S, S_<sup>-1</sup>_V<sub>j</sub>T, and T_<sup>-1</sup>_W<sub>j</sub>R have entries in_ \(\varepsilon\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\) _for all_ \(1\le j\le l\).

Unfortunately, unlike Theorem 2.1, the proof of this result is not constructive, meaning we cannot use it to find _R_, _S_, and _T_ algorithmically. As a result, it is typically easier to remove one term at a time. Possible generalizations capable of eliminating multiple terms simultaneously are discussed in Section 2.3.

## 2.2 Implementation Details and Results

We can use the results from the previous section to determine when an APA algorithm can be derived from an exact one. Nevertheless, the conditions suggested by Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.4 are more rare than we might expect. Indeed, an initial search of the repository of Sedoglavic<sup>8</sup> turned up no exact algorithms whose corresponding tensor decompositions contain a nilpotent term. Luckily we can generate more candidates by running a _flip graph_ search, which we describe below.

**Remark 2.5.** There are many other search algorithms for exact matrix multiplication that could be used here in place of the flip graph - e.g., algorithms that apply some version of least squares to the tensor decomposition problem \[3, 35, 56\] or use reinforcement/machine learning \[28, 47\]. We choose the flip-graph approach since it is particularly easy to use and requires minimal computing resources.

### 2.2.1 Flip Graph Search for Exact Decompositions

The flip graph is a recent tool for discovering (exact) matrix multiplication algorithms introduced by Kauers and Moosbauer \[39\]. For given _m_, _k_, and _n_, the vertices of the \(\langle m,k,n\rangle\) flip graph are \(\langle m,k,n\rangle\) matrix multiplication algorithms, represented by their corresponding tensor decompositions. Edges in the graph connect schemes that can be obtained from one another via the _flip_ operation. In the simplest case, a flip replaces two rank-one factors \(A\otimes B\otimes C\) and \(A\otimes B'\otimes C'\) in a matrix-multiplication decomposition with \(A\otimes(B+B')\otimes C\) and \(A\otimes B'\otimes(C'-C)\). Since this leaves the sum of the terms unchanged, each flip results in a new decomposition and corresponding algorithm (of the same rank). Note that this only works because the terms \(A\otimes B\otimes C\) and \(A\otimes B'\otimes C'\) share the common factor _A_; to perform a flip in general, we need at least one factor to be shared between the rank-one terms, though it need not be the first.

The key insight for Kauers and Moosbauer is that, under the right circumstances, an algorithm found in the flip graph can be _reduced_, meaning two rank-one terms can be replaced by a single one, thereby producing a new algorithm of lower rank. Accordingly, they propose a search algorithm that runs a "flip- graph walk," in which successive, random flips are applied to an initial decomposition, at each step checking for the conditions that make a reduction possible. In \[39\], they use this algorithm to improve the best-known ranks for several sizes \(\langle m,k,n\rangle\). Subsequent work accelerated the original flip graph algorithm by leveraging symmetry and/or traversing multiple sizes in one search \[1, 40, 46\].

In this work, we are interested in using a flip graph walk to generate many exact algorithms rather than improve the rank of exact matrix multiplication. In this way, the flip graph gives a simple search algorithm for our application: run a flip-graph walk, checking not for possible reductions but instead for decompositions that satisfy the conditions of Theorem 2.1 and/or Theorem 2.4. With this, we can now state our full algorithm for generating new APA schemes, which is shown here (in high-level pseudocode) as Algorithm 1. Like Theorem 2.2, this pseudocode assumes that the terms that can be removed from an exact decomposition are leading. This is done to simplify the notation (and since we can always reorder the terms in a decomposition however we like).

For better efficiency we use an implementation of Perminov \[50\] to execute the flip-graph search in line 1 of Algorithm 1. ### 2.2.2 Additional Results

In practice, the initial decompositions used to start the search are particularly important. Perminov’s implementation allows many flip graph walks to run in parallel, possibly with decompositions of different dimensions for each walk. Periodically, decompositions are combined or modified by meta-moves, as described in the meta-flip-graph paper \[40\]. With human intervention, we also chose the most promising decompositions seen so far as seeds for a restarted search. Most new border rank decompositions were found over the course of a week using a 23 thread search. We ran the search on a Ryzen 9 9900X CPU.

Our best result came in the case of \(\langle 2,4,5\rangle\), where we found the first rank 31 APA algorithm and therefore lowered the border rank upper bound for this size to 31. Encoding matrices for this algorithm are given in Section B.1. For the other schemes found in our search (including those listed in s 1 and 2), see https://github.com/nliskij/border-rank.

### 2.3 Generalization via Null Cone Membership Testing

Our approach to searching for suitable exact algorithms is not the most general possible. It may be the case that individual rank one terms cannot be made \(O(\varepsilon)\) but their sum can. In the representation theory literature, the sum of such terms would be called an element of the null cone of the De-Groote group. This may be promising for future work since recent papers have addressed algorithms for testing null cone membership \[14, 15\]. While such an approach can produce decompositions more general than described here, in practice we were not able to obtain any further border-rank improvements.

## 3 Alternative Basis APA Matrix Multiplication

In this section, we demonstrate that APA matrix multiplication algorithms can be accelerated by reducing their additive complexity, accomplished by applying fast, symbolic basis transformations to reduce the number of nonzero entries in the encoding matrices \(U(\varepsilon)\), \(V(\varepsilon)\) and \(W(\varepsilon)\) (recall Figure 2). This has the effect of lowering the leading coefficient in an APA algorithm’s arithmetic _and_ IO complexities.<sup>10</sup> In particular, generalizing \[32\], we present a greedy algorithm for constructing these basis transformations, which depend on an evaluation parameter \(\varepsilon\).

<sup>9</sup>This can be done since nilpotence of a product is simply a polynomial constraint in the entries of the corresponding matrices, which only requires adding additional rows to the Jacobian in the lifting step. <sup>10</sup>While not the focus of this paper, IO complexity refers to the amount of data movement or communication performed by an algorithm.

## 3.1 Background and Motivation

To outperform classical matrix multiplication in practice, the arithmetic and IO complexities of fast matrix multiplication algorithms must have small leading coefficients. To promote this, Karstadt and Schwartz \[38\] introduced alternative basis matrix multiplication, which takes an existing, exact algorithm and computes a set of basis transformations that sparsify the corresponding encoding matrices. That is, if \(U\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0k_0\times t}\), \(V\in\mathbb{C}^{k_0n_0\times t}\), and \(W\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0n_0\times t}\) are the encoding matrices of a \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0;t\rangle\) matrix multiplication scheme, the alternative basis method computes automorphisms \(\phi:\mathbb{C}^{m_0k_0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m_0k_0}\), \(\psi:\mathbb{C}^{k_0n_0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{k_0n_0}\), and \(\nu:\mathbb{C}^{m_0n_0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m_0n_0}\) and factors _U_, _V_ and _W_ as follows:

\(U=\phi\cdot U_\phi,V=\psi\cdot V_\psi,\text{and}W=\nu^{-1}\cdot W_\nu,\) (3.1)

where \(U_\phi\), \(V_\psi\), and \(W_\nu\) are sparse (or at least sparser than _U_, _V_ , and _W_). The key insight is the following: rewriting (1.7) as

\(c=W(U^Ta\odot V^Tb)=\nu^{-1}\left[W_\nu\left(U_\phi^T(\phi^Ta)\odot V_\psi^T(\psi^Tb)\right)\right]\) (3.2)

for _a_, _b_, and _c_ vectorized copies of \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0\times k_0}\), \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k_0\times n_0}\), and _C=AB_, we observe that \(\nu(C)\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0\times n_0}\) can be computed by applying the bilinear form represented by \(U_\phi\), \(V_\psi\) and \(W_\nu\) to the transformed inputs \(\phi(A)\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0\times k_0}\) and \(\psi(B)\in\mathbb{C}^{k_0\times n_0}\). Here, we use \(\phi(A)\), \(\psi(B)\), and \(\nu(C)\) to denote the matrices that, when vectorized, correspond to \(\phi^Ta\), \(\psi^Tb\), and \(\nu c\). Assuming that \(\phi(A)\), \(\psi(B)\) and _C_ can be obtained cheaply from _A_, _B_, and \(\nu(C)\), respectively, this offers a potentially much more efficient way of computing the output _C_. Note additionally that the basis transformations, like the corresponding encoding matrices, can be applied recursively for use on matrices of arbitrary size.

In \[38\], Karstadt and Schwartz used the alternative basis approach to reduce the leading coefficient in the arithmetic complexity of Strassen’s \(\langle 2,2,2;7\rangle\) algorithm to 5 without increasing communication costs, making it more practical than \[16\]. Efforts to apply this technique to other fast exact algorithms quickly followed \[6, 7, 29\]. Corresponding implementations show CPU and GPU speedups for the resulting alternative basis algorithms (e.g., \[13, 25, 37, 52, 54\]). In all of these, fast basis transformations are used, which can be applied recursively to \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\), \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) and \(C\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}\) at the modest overhead cost of _O(mk_log(_mk_)), _O(kn_log(_kn_)), and _O(mn_log(_mn_)) flops, respectively (see \[38, Section 2.1\]).

Extending this work to the APA setting is relatively straightforward. Given a set of encoding matrices \(U(\varepsilon)\), \(V(\varepsilon)\), and \(W(\varepsilon)\) for \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0;t\rangle\) APA matrix multiplication, we seek symbolic basis transformations \(\phi_\varepsilon\), \(\psi_\varepsilon\), and \(\nu_\varepsilon\) such that

\(U(\varepsilon)=\phi_\varepsilon\cdot U_\phi(\varepsilon),V(\varepsilon)=\psi_\varepsilon\cdot V_\psi(\varepsilon),\text{and}W(\varepsilon)=\nu_\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot W_\nu(\varepsilon),\) (3.3)

where \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon)\), and \(W_\nu(\varepsilon)\) are the (parser) encoding matrices of an APA bilinear form in the bases \(\phi_\varepsilon\), \(\psi_\varepsilon\), \(\nu_\varepsilon\). These can then be used to generate an Alternative Basis APA Matrix Multiplication algorithm, which is shown here as Algorithm 2.

**Algorithm 2** Alternative Basis APA Matrix Multiplication (**AltBasis-Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle}\))

**Input:** \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\), \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\), and \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{C}\).

**Output:** \(M=AB+\varepsilon R_1+\varepsilon^2R_2+\cdots+\varepsilon^{p-1}R_{p-1}\) for residual matrices \(R_1,\dots,R_{p-1}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}\) and _p=dL_+1.

1: \(\widetilde{A}=\phi_\varepsilon(A)\)

2: \(\widetilde{B}=\psi_\varepsilon(B)\)

3: \(\widetilde{M}=\text{\textbf{Recursive-APA}}_{\langle U_\phi(\varepsilon),V_\psi(\varepsilon),W_\nu(\varepsilon)\rangle}(\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B})\)

4: \(M=\nu_\varepsilon^{-1}(\widetilde{M})\)

5: **return** _M_

In this pseudocode, **Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle U_\phi(\varepsilon),V_\psi(\varepsilon),W_\nu(\varepsilon)\rangle}(\widetilde{A},\widetilde{B})\) evaluates the recursive bilinear form corre sponding to \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon)\), and \(W_\nu(\varepsilon)\) at the transformed inputs \(\widetilde{A}\) and \(\widetilde{B}\), obtained by applying \(\phi_\varepsilon\) and \(\psi_\varepsilon\) to _A_ and _B_. Following the notation from the previous section, _d_ is the degree of the underlying APA matrix multiplication algorithm and _L_ is the number of recursive steps applied. The complexity of Algorithm 2, in terms of _t_ and the sparsity of \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon)\), and \(W_\nu(\varepsilon)\) and including the cost of the basis transformations, follows from the exact case - e.g., \[32, 38\].

## 3.2 Symbolic Sparsification

One question remains: how do we obtain the symbolic basis transformations \(\phi_\varepsilon\), \(\psi_\varepsilon\) and \(\nu_\varepsilon\)? In this work, we use a symbolic version of the greedy sparsification algorithm first proposed by Holtz et al. \[32\], which, in the context of fast exact matrix multiplication, is capable of producing optimal (in terms of resulting sparsity) basis transformations and has been shown to reduce the leading coefficient of an algorithm’s arithmetic complexity by up to 89%. Our symbolic version is shown here as Algorithm 3. For simplicity we restrict our focus to \(U(\varepsilon)\), but the algorithm applies identically to \(V(\varepsilon)\) and \(W(\varepsilon)\).

**Algorithm 3** Symbolic Sparsification Algorithm

**Input:** \(U(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]^{m_0k_0\times t}\) with \(\mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)}(U(\varepsilon))=m_0k_0\) and a constant \(r\in\mathbb{R}^+\).

**Output:** Invertible \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\in\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]^{m_0k_0\times m_0k_0}\) such that \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)=\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}U(\varepsilon)\) is as sparse as possible.

1: \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}=\emptyset\)

2: \(w_c=\mathbf{Generate-Constraints}(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1})\)

3: **for** \(i=1:r\cdot t\) **do**

4: **while** \(\mathbf{Next-Vector}(i,w_c)\neq\emptyset\) **do**

5: _v_=**Next-Vector**(_i,w<sub>c</sub>_)

6: \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}=[\phi_\varepsilon^{-1};v^T]\)

7: _w<sub>c</sub>_=**Generate-Constraints** (\(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\))

8: **if** \(\mathrm{size}(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1},1)=m_0k_0\) **then**

9: **return** \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\)

10: **end if**

11: **end while**

12: **end for**

Algorithm 3 progressively constructs a set of vectors \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\) in \(\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]^{m_0k_0}\) according to the following rules: (1) each newly added vector _v_ should be linearly independent to the current collection and (2) \(v^TU(\varepsilon)\) should be as sparse as possible. This is done via the following subroutines:

1. **Generate-Constraints**\((\phi_\varepsilon^{-1})\) - returns a set of constraints _w<sub>c</sub>_ that, when satisfied by a vector \(v\in\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]^{m_0k_0}\), implies that it is linearly independent to every (row) vector in \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\).<tbc>

2. **Next-Vector**(_i,w<sub>c</sub>_) - returns a vector \(v\in\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]^{m_0k_0}\) that satisfies both the constraints _w<sub>c</sub>_ and \(\mathrm{weight}(v^TU(\varepsilon))=i\).<tbc>

<tbc>For the latter, the function \(\mathrm{weight}(\cdot)\) is a measure of sparsity defined as

\(\mathrm{weight}(v^TU(\varepsilon)):=\mathrm{nnz}(v^TU(\varepsilon))+\mathrm{nns}(v^TU(\varepsilon))+\mathrm{nnc}(v^TU(\varepsilon))\cdot p,\) (3.4)

where nnz is the number of nonzero entries, nns is the number of constant, nonsingleton entries (that is, not -1, 0, or 1), and nnc is the number of variable entries, i.e., that contain \(\varepsilon\), for _p_ a tunable parameter. (3.4) naturally extends to the matrix \(U(\varepsilon)\) as follows

\(\mathrm{weight}(U(\varepsilon)):=\mathrm{nnz}(U(\varepsilon))+\mathrm{nns}(U(\varepsilon))+\mathrm{nnc}(U(\varepsilon))\cdot p-\mathrm{ncols}(U(\varepsilon)),\) (3.5)

where ncols is the number of columns.<sup>11</sup> By repeatedly calling **Next-Vector** for increasing values of _i_, Algorithm 3 promotes optimal sparsity; that is, each newly added vector _v_ has the smallest value of \(\mathrm{weight}(v^TU(\varepsilon))\) possible. Accordingly, the constant _r_ should be chosen so that \(r\cdot t\) is the maximum possible value of \(\mathrm{weight}(v^TU(\varepsilon))\), specifically to guarantee that the algorithm terminates.

Importantly, we have made several simplifications here both for convenience and to accelerate Algorithm 3. We summarize them below.

1. First, we assume that the encoding matrix \(U(\varepsilon)\) belongs to \(\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]^{m_0k_0\times t}\), equivalently that its entries are Laurent polynomials in \(\varepsilon\) as opposed to arbitrary rational functions in \(\varepsilon\). Similarly, **Next-Vector** returns \(v\in\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]^{m_0k_0}\). We focus on Laurent polynomials for the following reasons: (1) essentially all<tbc>

<sup>11</sup>In the case of \(\mathrm{weight}(W(\varepsilon))\), ncols is replaced by nrows, the number of rows in \(W(\varepsilon)\).

APA algorithms in the literature - including those derived in Section 2 - have encoding matrices with Laurent polynomial entries and (2) restricting the search to \(\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]\) greatly improves its efficiency without sacrificing sparsity (see Theorem 3.2). Note that, while this ultimately implies that \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\) will have Laurent-polynomial entries, its inverse \(\phi_\varepsilon\) (which recall is necessary to evaluate Algorithm 2) may contain rational entries.<tbc>

2. Second, we choose not to differentiate between different kinds of variable entries in our measure of sparsity - i.e., a simple monomial entry like \(\varepsilon^2\) and a much more complicated Laurent polynomial contribute the same to (3.4) and (3.5). We justify this choice by noting that, when running Algorithm 2, any variable entries in the encoding matrices/basis transformations can be computed ahead of time at minor additional cost (that will not contribute to the leading-term complexity of the algorithm). Of course, Algorithm 3 can be run with a different definition of weight\((\cdot)\), if desired.

As mentioned above, the parameter _p_ is tunable and in particular determines how much to penalize variable entries in \(v^TU(\varepsilon)\). Choosing a large value of _p_ can often lead to basis transformations that eliminate \(\varepsilon\) terms entirely, in which case \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon)\), and \(W_\nu(\varepsilon)\) in (3.3) are constant (see, e.g., Section 3.2.3).

## 3.2.1 Implementation Details

There are a handful of technical questions concerning Algorithm 3 that we address below:

1. How does **Generate-Constraints** work? In Theorem 3.1, we demonstrate that it is sufficient to define constraints in terms of a basis for the kernel of \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\).<tbc>

2. Is Algorithm 3 well-posed - i.e., can **Next-Vector** always find a solution with Laurent-polynomial entries? Moreover, can this be done without sacrificing sparsity? Theorem 3.2 verifies that the answer to both is yes (under certain conditions).

We start with the subroutine **Generate-Constraints**, which can be implemented by computing a basis for the kernel of \(\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\) (in the vector space \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^n\)) and subsequently defining the set of constraints as those that guarantee that the next vector _v_ has a nontrivial inner product with at least one of these basis vectors. This follows from a basic linear algebra result (see e.g., \[32, Theorem 3.2\]), which we state here for \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)\).

**Proposition 3.1.** _Let_ \(v_1,\dots,v_m\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^n\) _and let_ \(A\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^{m\times n}\) _be the matrix whose i-th row is_ \(v_i^T\)_. Suppose that q_<sub>1</sub>_,...,q<sub>r</sub> form a basis for the kernel of A and let_ \(v\in\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)^n\)_. In this case,_ \(v\notin\mathrm{span}\left\{v_1,\dots,v_m\right\}\) _if and only if_ \(q_i^Tv\neq 0\) _for at least one i. Hence, kernel basis vectors of A can be used to certify the independence of v from the rows of A._

This can be used to further accelerate the Algorithm 3 - e.g., by providing Z3 with a narrower range of exponents to search over. Of course, for this to be usable we need to bound _H_ and _k_. This can be done by applying the following identity to the \(\Delta_i(\varepsilon)\).

**Proposition 3.3** (Hilbert nullstellensatz)**.** _Let_ \(f_1,\dots,f_m\in\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\)_, and let D_=max_<sub>i</sub>_deg_f<sub>i</sub>. If_

\(gcd(f_1,\dots,f_m)=1\) (3.16)

_then there exist polynomials_ \(a_1(\varepsilon),\dots,a_m(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\) _such that_ \(\sum_{i=1}^ma_i(\varepsilon)f_i(\varepsilon)=1\) _where_ \(dega_i\le max\{3,D\}\) _for every i._

_Proof._ This is a classical result in algebraic geometry. For the degree bound, see \[43\].

In particular, suppose that \(g(\varepsilon)=gcd(\Delta_1(\varepsilon),\dots,\Delta_m(\varepsilon))\). Since Theorem 3.2 assumes that the ideal generated by the \(\Delta_i(\varepsilon)\) contains a monomial, \(g(\varepsilon)\) divides a monomial and is therefore one itself (up to a nonzero scalar). With this in mind, write \(g(\varepsilon)=c\varepsilon^r\) for some \(c\neq 0\) and \(r\ge 0\). Since \(g(\varepsilon)\) divides the \(\Delta_i(\varepsilon)\), and recalling that each \(\Delta_i(\varepsilon)\) has degree at most \(\rho(\beta-\alpha)\), we have

\(0\le r\le\rho(\beta-\alpha).\) (3.17)

For each _i_, write \(\Delta_i(\varepsilon)=c\varepsilon^rf_i(\varepsilon)\). By construction, gcd(_f_<sub>1</sub>_,...,f<sub>m</sub>_)=1 and

\(degf_i=deg\Delta_i-r\le\rho(\beta-\alpha)-r,\) (3.18)

so Theorem 3.3 implies that there exist polynomials \(a_i(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]\) such that \(\sum_ia_i(\varepsilon)f_i(\varepsilon)=1\) and \(dega_i\le\rho(\beta-\alpha)-r\). Multiplying by \(c\varepsilon^r\), we obtain

\(\sum_ia_i(\varepsilon)\Delta_i(\varepsilon)=c\varepsilon^r.\) (3.19)

Thus, in Theorem 3.2, we can take _k=r_ and \(H\le max\{3,\rho(\beta-\alpha)-r\}\). Notice that, because we simply need to keep the constants the same to have a vector with same or better weight, we can set _B_<sub>-</sub>=_B_<sub>+</sub>=0.

## 3.2.2 Optimality

With the above results, Algorithm 3 is guaranteed to achieve optimal sparsity, as measured by (3.4) and (3.5), under the assumption that **Next-Vector** returns an admissible vector whenever one exists (guaranteed as long as the first condition of Theorem 3.2 holds for the corresponding encoding matrix). This can be shown by simply replicating the optimality proof from \[32\], interpreting the notations of span, rank, and independence as defined over \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)\). Note that this still holds under alternative definitions of \(weight(\cdot)\), meaning Algorithm 3 is adaptable to other notions of sparsity.

### 3.2.3 Sparsifying Algorithms Obtained by Term Deletion

We close this subsection by considering the sparsification of the APA algorithms obtained from the search procedure discussed in Section 2. These algorithms have special structure: their parameter dependence comes from a De-Groote transformation applied to an exact decomposition. As a result, verified below, we can always construct alternative bases whose corresponding encoding matrices \(U_\phi\), \(V_\psi\), and \(W_\nu\) are independent of \(\varepsilon\). Moreover, this does not come at the expense of sparsity (again, as measured by weight\((\cdot)\)).

**Proposition 3.4.** _Let_ \(U(\varepsilon)\), \(V(\varepsilon)\)_, and_ \(W(\varepsilon)\) _be obtained from an exact algorithm as in Section 2. Consider any invertible, symbolic alternative-basis transformations_ \(\phi_\varepsilon\), \(\psi_\varepsilon\)_, and_ \(\nu_\varepsilon\) _for which the encoding matrices_

\(U_\phi(\varepsilon)=\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot U(\varepsilon),V_\psi(\varepsilon)=\psi_\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot V(\varepsilon),W_\nu(\varepsilon)=\nu_\varepsilon\cdot W(\varepsilon)\)

_have Laurent-polynomial entries. The following hold:_

1. _There are equivalent alternative-basis transformations_ \(\tilde{\phi}_\varepsilon\), \(\tilde{\psi}_\varepsilon\)_, and_ \(\tilde{\nu}_\varepsilon\) _for which_ \(U_\tilde{\phi}(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\tilde{\psi}(\varepsilon)\)_, and_ \(W_\tilde{\nu}(\varepsilon)\) _are constant. The maps_ \(\tilde{\phi}_\varepsilon^{-1}\), \(\tilde{\psi}_\varepsilon^{-1}\)_, and_ \(\tilde{\nu}_\varepsilon\) _have Laurent-polynomial entries._<tbc>

_2._ _If the parameter p in_ (3.4) _satisfies_ \(p\ge 1\)_, the weight of each constant encoding matrix is no greater than that of its original counterpart._

_Proof._ We prove both claims for \(U(\varepsilon)\). Let _U_ be the encoding matrix of the parent decomposition after the selected terms have been deleted. With the row-wise vectorization used here, set \(D_\varepsilon=R^{-1}\otimes S^T\), where _R_ and _S_ are the De-Groote transformations from Section 2. Then \(U(\varepsilon)=D_\varepsilon U\), and \(D_\varepsilon\) and \(D_\varepsilon^{-1}\) have Laurent-polynomial entries. Set<tbc>

\(G_\varepsilon=\phi_\varepsilon^{-1}D_\varepsilon.\) (3.20)

<tbc>Because the coefficient field is infinite and \(G_\varepsilon\) is invertible over \(\mathbb{C}(\varepsilon)\), we can choose a nonzero \(\varepsilon_0\) at which \(G_{\varepsilon_0}\) is defined and invertible. Define<tbc>

\(\tilde{\phi}_\varepsilon^{-1}=G_{\varepsilon_0}D_\varepsilon^{-1}.\) (3.21)

<tbc>This map has Laurent-polynomial entries, and

\(U_\tilde{\phi}(\varepsilon)=\tilde{\phi}_\varepsilon^{-1}U(\varepsilon)=G_{\varepsilon_0}U\) (3.22)

is constant. Moreover, \(U_\tilde{\phi}(\varepsilon)\) is obtained by evaluating \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)=G_\varepsilon U\) at \(\varepsilon_0\). Hence, every constant entry retains its value, and every nonconstant entry becomes a constant. This implies that the weight cannot increase. For \(V(\varepsilon)\) and \(W(\varepsilon)\), the proof is the same, using \(\psi_\varepsilon^{-1}\) and \(\nu_\varepsilon\), respectively, as the maps that produce their encoding matrices.

The benefit of sparsifying this way (when possible) is straightforward: if \(U_\phi\), \(V_\psi\), and \(W_\nu\) have no \(\varepsilon\) dependence, then we can perform the approximate-to-exact procedure of Bini \[9\] by applying several basis transformations in parallel before evaluating the bilinear algorithm corresponding to \(U_\phi\), \(V_\psi\), and \(W_\nu\) in a batched fashion.

## 3.3 Results

To evaluate the arithmetic complexity of the resulting algorithms, we compute the leading coefficients using the framework of \[32\]. For each sparsified algorithm, we first compute the base-case linear-operation counts _q<sub>U</sub>_, _q<sub>V</sub>_, and _q<sub>W</sub>_ of its encoding and decoding matrices. In the APA setting, these counts are evaluated symbolically in \(\varepsilon\), and we use _p_=2 for the weight calculation in (3.4). We then apply the recursion-order optimization of \[32\], which uses dynamic programming to evaluate recursive compositions of the algorithm and its permutations for square matrix multiplication. Among the resulting recursion orders, we report the minimum leading coefficient returned by this procedure. An example is given in Section B.3.

The sparsification results recorded in  2 were obtained on a laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 9. Most encoding matrices could be successfully sparsified after running Algorithm 3 for less than an hour. Only three required a run time of more than a day: two completed in two days and the last in three. While, in general, larger matrices took longer to sparsify, this is not the only factor determining the run time of Algorithm 3. In fact, it seems that the complexity of the matrix entries matter more than the size of the matrix.

## 4 APA Matrix Multiplication is Stable

In this section, we show that alternative basis APA matrix multiplication is stable by proving a (weak) forward error bound for a floating-point implementation of the approximate-to-exact procedure represented by Algorithm 4. In line three of this algorithm, **AltBasis-Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle}\) is a recursive implementation of an alternative basis APA matrix multiplication routine (i.e, Algorithm 2), indexed by the corresponding symbolic basis transformations \(\phi\), \(\psi\), and \(\nu\). Following the previous section, this algorithm is based on an alternative basis \(\langle m_0,k_0,n_0;t\rangle\) scheme defined by parameterized encoding matrices \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon)\) and \(W_\nu(\varepsilon)\).

**Algorithm 4** Approximate-to-Exact Alternative Basis APA Matrix Multiplication

**Input:** \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\), \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) and parameters \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\in\mathbb{C}\), where _p=dL_+1.

**Output:** _C=AB_.

1: \([\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_p]=\text{\textbf{Vandermonde-Solve}}(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p)\)

2: **for** _j_=1:_p_ **do**

3: \(C_j=\text{\textbf{AltBasis-Recursive-APA}}_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle}(A,B,\varepsilon_j)\)

4: **end for**

5: \(C=\alpha_1C_1+\alpha_2C_2+\cdots+\alpha_pC_p\)

6: **return** _C_

As discussed in the introduction, Algorithm 4 obtains the exact product of _A_ and _B_ by evaluating **AltBasis-Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle} p=dL+1\) times with different values of \(\varepsilon\) and taking a linear combination of the output (after applying the corresponding basis transformation \(\nu_\varepsilon\)). The coefficients in this linear combination solve the Vandermonde system (1.5) with _p_ replacing _d_ and are computed in line 1 of Algorithm 4 by the routine **Vandermonde-Solve**. Note that each \(\alpha_j\) can be expressed in terms of \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\) as follows:

\(\alpha_j=(-1)^{p-1}\prod_{k\neq j}\frac{\varepsilon_k}{\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_k}=\prod_{k\neq j}\frac{\varepsilon_k}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j}.\) (4.1)

We also have the special case \(\alpha_j=1/p\) for all _j_ when the \(\varepsilon_i\) are the _p_-th roots of unity.

To obtain a forward error bound for a floating-point implementation of Algorithm 4 we extend work of Schwartz et al. \[53\] to the APA setting. The results of \[53\] are the most recent in a long line of research on the stability of fast matrix multiplication, which traces its roots back to work of Brent \[12\] and Bini and Lotti \[11\]. The normwise stability bounds derived by these authors for specific algorithms - i.e., the same notion of weak forward stability established for APA algorithms in this paper (see Theorem 4.6) - was eventually shown to apply to the broad class of fast (exact) matrix multiplication routines by Demmel et al. \[21\]. The contribution of Schwartz et al. in \[53\], itself a generalization of \[2\], was to extend this framework to include alternative basis matrix multiplication \[32\], and hence their bounds are a natural fit for our setting in light of the previous section. To the best of our knowledge, the results presented here are the first stability bounds derived for APA matrix multiplication.

**Remark 4.1.** The bounds presented in this section are stated in terms of the maximum-entry norm - i.e., \(\|A\|=max_{ij}|A(i,j)|\). This matches most of the results in the literature on the stability of fast matrix multiplication. Dumas, Pernet, and Sedoglavic \[25\], however, recently derived new bounds in terms of arbitrary norms, which are tighter than what can be obtained by simply applying norm equivalence. They demonstrate the efficacy of their bounds by using them to obtain algorithms that are more stable in practice (including with respect to the maximum entry norm). Since our goal in this section is to demonstrate stability for Algorithm 4, we leave an APA extension of these results to future work. Similarly, we do not consider scaling techniques (e.g., \[26\]), even though this is a well-documented way to further improve the stability of fast exact matrix multiplication (see the discussion in \[23\]).

### 4.1 Preliminaries

We begin by summarizing the building blocks of our analysis. Throughout, we adopt a standard model for floating-point arithmetic \[31, 48\], in which each binary floating-point operation \(\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}\) satisfies

\(fl(x\circ y)=(x\circ y)(1+\delta)\text{for some}|\delta|\le\text{\textbf{u}},\) (4.2)

where \(fl(x\circ y)\) and \(x\circ y\) are the floating-point and exact outputs, respectively, and **u** is the _unit roundoff_. Every operation in Algorithm 4, including the evaluation of the symbolic encoding matrices and the application of the fast basis transformations, incurs this floating-point error. In addition, we assume that the coefficients \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_p\) are computed to high _relative_ accuracy in line one - i.e., if \(\widehat{\alpha}_1,\dots,\widehat{\alpha}_p\) are the outputs of \(\mathbf{Vandermonde-Solve}(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p)\) in floating-point arithmetic and \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_p\) are the corresponding exact quantities, then

\(\frac{|\widehat{\alpha}_j-\alpha_j|}{|\alpha_j|}\le\delta\) (4.3)

for some small \(\delta>0\). Theorem A.1 demonstrates that this holds for \(\delta=O(\mathbf{u})\), under some mild conditions, if the \(\alpha_j\) are obtained by evaluating (4.1) directly. Of course, this is not the only way to handle the first step of Algorithm 4 (see for example \[30, 31\]) though it is sufficient for our purposes.

Ultimately, the performance of Algorithm 4 does not depend critically on how the Vandermonde system is solved. After all, the coefficients \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_p\) could be computed ahead of time in higher precision if needed. Nevertheless, Theorem A.1 foreshadows how the stability of alternative basis APA matrix multiplication depends on the choice of \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\). In the worst cases - for example, when the \(\varepsilon_i\) are large/small or tightly clustered - it will be difficult to avoid under/overflow when evaluating (4.1). On the flip side, if the \(\varepsilon_i\) are roots of unity then we can skip **Vandermonde-Solve** altogether, as the corresponding coefficients \(\alpha_j=1/p\) are known exactly.

The final ingredient of our analysis is an error bound of Schwartz et al. \[53\], which covers a single evaluation of an alternative basis APA matrix multiplication routine (that is, Algorithm 2). To state this result, we need the following definitions. Note that Theorem 4.3 and Theorem 4.4 generalize \[53, Definition 3.4\] and \[53, Definition 3.2\], respectively.

**Definition 4.2.** The _error accumulation operator ⋆_ takes as input a vector \(v\in\mathbb{C}^m\) and a matrix \(M\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}\) and outputs \(v\star M\in\mathbb{C}^n\) satisfying

\(v\star M=\left(\begin{array}{ c }
\mathrm{nnz}(M(:,1))+\|v\odot\mathbb{I}(M(:,1))\|_\infty \\
\mathrm{nnz}(M(:,2))+\|v\odot\mathbb{I}(M(:,2))\|_\infty \\
\vdots \\
\mathrm{nnz}(M(:,n))+\|v\odot\mathbb{I}(M(:,n))\|_\infty
\end{array}\right),\)

where \(\odot\) is the Hadamard product and where \(\mathrm{nnz}(w)\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\mathbb{I}(w)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) are, respectively, the number of nonzero entries in the vector \(w\in\mathbb{C}^n\) and a vector that records whether each entry of _w_ is nonzero - that is, the _i_-th entry of I(_w_) is one if _w<sub>i</sub>_ is nonzero and zero otherwise. Following \[53\], we also use the shorthand notation ⋆_M_:=0⋆_M_ for 0 the zero vector.

**Definition 4.3.** Let \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon)\), and \(W_\nu(\varepsilon)\) be the encoding matrices of an alternative basis APA matrix multiplication algorithm with associated basis transformations \(\phi_\varepsilon\), \(\psi_\varepsilon\), and \(\nu_\varepsilon^{-1}\). Define the vectors \(a_\varepsilon\) and \(b_\varepsilon\) as follows:<tbc>

\(a_\varepsilon=\left(|\phi_\varepsilon|\cdot|U_\phi(\varepsilon)|\right)^T\mathbb{1}\text{and}b_\varepsilon=\left(|\psi_\varepsilon|\cdot|V_\psi(\varepsilon)|\right)^T\mathbb{1},\)

<tbc>where 1 is a vector of all ones (of the appropriate dimension). The algorithm’s _stability vector_ \(e_\varepsilon\) is then

\(e_\varepsilon=\left(|\nu_\varepsilon^{-1}|\cdot|W_\nu(\varepsilon)|\right)(a_\varepsilon\odot b_\varepsilon)\)

where \(\odot\) represents the Hadamard product. The corresponding _stability factor_ is \(E(\varepsilon)=\|e_\varepsilon\|_\infty\).

**Definition 4.4.** Let \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon)\), and \(W_\nu(\varepsilon)\) be the encoding matrices of an alternative basis APA matrix multiplication algorithm with associated basis transformations \(\phi_\varepsilon\), \(\psi_\varepsilon\), and \(\nu_\varepsilon^{-1}\). Define the vector

\(q_\varepsilon=\left((\star\phi_\varepsilon\star U_\phi(\varepsilon))+(\star\psi_\varepsilon\star V_\psi(\varepsilon))\right)\star W_\nu(\varepsilon)^T\star\nu_\varepsilon^{-T}.\)

The _stability prefactor_ of the algorithm is then \(Q(\varepsilon)=\|q_\varepsilon\|_\infty\).

Note that the stability factor \(E(\varepsilon)\) can be used to bound the norm of the output of a recursive APA algorithm. Indeed, if _C_ is the output of Algorithm 2 (which defaults to exact matrix multiplication after _L_ recursive steps) in exact arithmetic, then<tbc>

\(\|C\|\le(k/k_0^L)E(\varepsilon)^L\|A\|\|B\|\) (4.4)

for \(\|\cdot\|\) the maximum-entry norm. This follows from (3.2), applied recursively, and was similarly observed by Schwartz et al. in the proof of \[53, Theorem 4.5\].

The focus of \[53\] is alternative basis _exact_ matrix multiplication (in the same model of floating-point arithmetic and using analogous definitions of stability factor/prefactor). Since their analysis does not assume that the bilinear form being evaluated is exact matrix multiplication, their bound immediately extends to the APA setting. Only one modification is necessary: the encoding matrices, basis transformations, and stability factor/prefactor now depend on the evaluation parameter \(\varepsilon\). We state a modified version of their main result below.

**Theorem 4.5** (Schwartz et al. \[53\])**.** _Let_ \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\) _and_ \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) _and suppose that_ \(\widehat{C}\) _and C are the floating- point and exact arithmetic outputs of a recursive, alternative basis APA matrix multiplication algorithm (i.e., Algorithm 2) evaluated at_ \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{C}\)_. If the base case of this algorithm multiplies_ \(m_0\times k_0\) _and_ \(k_0\times n_0\) _matrices, then we have_

\(\|\widehat{C}-C\|\le\left(k/k_0^L+Q(\varepsilon)L\right)\left(k/k_0^L\right)E(\varepsilon)^L\|A\|\|B\|\mathbf{u}+O(\mathbf{u}^2),\)

_where L is the required number of recursive steps,_ \(\|\cdot\|\) _is the maximum entry norm, and_ \(E(\varepsilon)\) _and_ \(Q(\varepsilon)\) _are the stability factor and prefactor of the algorithm, respectively._

## 4.2 Main Error Bound

We now prove the main result of this section, which exhibits (weak) forward stability for Algorithm 4 under some mild assumptions on the inputs and the two subroutines **Vandermonde-Solve** and **AltBasis- Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle}\). The main insight of the proof is that Theorem 4.5 can be used to bound the error in a single evaluation of **AltBasis-Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle}\) and moreover that this implies stability for Algorithm 4 when combined with the following observations:

• In the APA setting, the encoding matrices and basis transformations have functional entries, which must be evaluated at each evaluation point \(\varepsilon_j\). Nevertheless, if these entries are computed to high relative accuracy then only minor additional error is introduced (see Theorem A.3).<tbc>

• The sum reduction in line 5 is similarly unproblematic if **Vandermonde-Solve** satisfies (4.3).

Accordingly, Theorem 4.6 is stated in terms of two parameters \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\), which denote how accurately (in terms of relative error) the solution to the Vandermonde system and the entries of the encoding matrices/basis transformations are computed. We choose to leave these as tunable parameters since, in practice, both the \(\alpha_j\) and the entries of \(U_\phi(\varepsilon_j)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon_j)\), \(W_\nu(\varepsilon_j)\), \(\phi_{\varepsilon_j}\), \(\psi_{\varepsilon_j}\) and \(\nu_{\varepsilon_j}^{-1}\) can be computed offline to whatever precision is desired (without changing the asymptotic cost of Algorithm 4). Recall that Theorem A.1 implies that \(\delta_1\) can be replaced with 3_p_**u**+_O_(**u**<sup>2</sup>) if we simply evaluate (4.1) directly.

**Theorem 4.6.** _Let_ \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\) _and_ \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) _with C=AB. Suppose that_ \(\widehat{C}\) _is the output of a floating-point implementation of Algorithm 4 under the following conditions:_

1. _Both the entries of A and B and the evaluation parameters_ \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\in\mathbb{C}\) _are normalized floating-point numbers. In addition, the_ \(\varepsilon_i\) _are nonzero with_ \(\varepsilon_i\neq\varepsilon_j\) _if_ \(i\neq j\).<tbc>

_2._ **Vandermonde-Solve** _satisfies the relative error bound_ (4.3) _for some small constant_ \(\delta_1>0\).<tbc>

_3._ **AltBasis-Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle}\) _implements a recursive, alternative basis APA matrix multiplication algorithm, defined by encoding matrices_ \(U_\phi(\varepsilon)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon)\), \(W_\nu(\varepsilon)\) _and symbolic basis transformations_ \(\phi_\varepsilon\), \(\psi_\varepsilon\), \(\nu_\varepsilon^{-1}\)_. The base case of this algorithm, which is reached after_ \(L\in\mathbb{N}\) _recursive steps for_<tbc>

<tbc>\(L\le min\left\{log_{m_0}(m),log_{k_0}(k),log_{n_0}(n)\right\},\)<tbc>

<tbc>_defaults to classical matrix multiplication. We additionally assume that_ \(m_0^L\), \(k_0^L\)_, and_ \(n_0^L\) _divide m, k, and n, respectively._<tbc>

_4._ _For each_ \(\varepsilon_i\)_, the nonzero entries of_ \(U_\phi(\varepsilon_i)\), \(V_\psi(\varepsilon_i)\), \(W_\nu(\varepsilon_i)\), \(\phi_{\varepsilon_i}\), \(\psi_{\varepsilon_i}\)_, and_ \(\nu_{\varepsilon_i}^{-1}\) _belong to the normalized range of the floating-point system and are computed to relative accuracy_ \(\delta_2\) _for some_ \(0<\delta_2<1\).<tbc>

<tbc>_Then we have_<tbc>

\(\|\widehat{C}-C\|\le(k/k_0^L)\left[\sum_{j=1}^p\left(\prod_{i\neq j}\frac{|\varepsilon_i|}{|\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j|}\right)(g(\delta_1,\delta_2)f(\varepsilon_j)\mathbf{u}+(g(\delta_1,\delta_2)-1))E(\varepsilon_j)^L\right]\|A\|\|B\|+O(\mathbf{u}^2)\)

\(f(\varepsilon_j)=(k/k_0^L)+Q(\varepsilon_j)L+\lceil log_2p\rceil+1\text{\textit{and}}g(\delta_1,\delta_2)=(1+\delta_2)^{6L}(1+\delta_1),\)

_where_ \(\|\cdot\|\) _is the maximum-entry norm,_ **u** _is the unit roundoff, and_ \(E(\varepsilon)\) _and_ \(Q(\varepsilon)\) _are the stability factor and prefactor, respectively, of_ **AltBasis-Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle}\).

_Proof._ Let \(\widehat{\alpha}_1,\dots,\widehat{\alpha}_p\in\mathbb{C}\) and \(\widehat{C}_j\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}\) be the floating-point output of **Vandermonde-Solve**\((\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p)\) and **AltBasis-Recursive-APA**\(_{\langle\phi,\psi,\nu\rangle}(A,B,\varepsilon_j)\), respectively. If \(\sum_{j=1}^p\widehat{\alpha}_j\widehat{C}_j\) is the _exact_ linear combination of the floating-point quantities \(\widehat{\alpha}_j\) and \(\widehat{C}_j\), and if \(\widetilde{C}_j\) is the exact- arithmetic output of the recursive, alternative basis bilinear algorithm corresponding to \(\widetilde{U}_\phi(\varepsilon_j)\), \(\widetilde{V}_\psi(\varepsilon_j)\), \(\widetilde{W}_\nu(\varepsilon_j)\), \(\tilde{\phi}_{\varepsilon_j}\), \(\tilde{\psi}_{\varepsilon_j}\), and \(\tilde{\nu}_{\varepsilon_j}^{-1}\), then we have

\(\|\widehat{C}-C\|=\left\|\widehat{C}-\sum_{j=1}^p\widehat{\alpha}_j\widehat{C}_j+\sum_{j=1}^p\widehat{\alpha}_j\widehat{C}_j-\sum_{j=1}^p\alpha_jC_j\right\|\le\left\|\widehat{C}-\sum_{j=1}^p\widehat{\alpha}_j\widehat{C}_j\right\|+\sum_{j=1}^p\|\widehat{\alpha}_j\widehat{C}_j-\alpha_jC_j\|,\) (4.5)

\(\sum_{j=1}^p\|\widehat{\alpha}_j\widehat{C}_j-\alpha_jC_j\|=\sum_{j=1}^p\|\widehat{\alpha}_j\widehat{C}_j-\widehat{\alpha}_j\widetilde{C}_j+\widehat{\alpha}_j\widetilde{C}_j-\alpha_j\widetilde{C}_j+\alpha_j\widetilde{C}_j-\alpha_jC_j\|\le\sum_{j=1}^p\left(|\widehat{\alpha}_j|\|\widehat{C}_j-\widetilde{C}_j\|+|\widehat{\alpha}_j-\alpha_j|\|\widetilde{C}_j\|+|\alpha_j|\|\widetilde{C}_j-C_j\|\right)\le\sum_{j=1}^p\left(|\alpha_j|\left(\|\widehat{C}_j-\widetilde{C}_j\|+\|\widetilde{C}_j-C_j\|\right)+|\widehat{\alpha}_j-\alpha_j|\left(\|\widetilde{C}_j\|+\|\widehat{C}_j-\widetilde{C}_j\|\right)\right)\le\sum_{j=1}^p\left(|\alpha_j|\left(\|\widehat{C}_j-\widetilde{C}_j\|+\|\widetilde{C}_j-C_j\|+\delta_1\left(\|\widetilde{C}_j\|+\|\widehat{C}_j-\widetilde{C}_j\|\right)\right)\right)=\sum_{j=1}^p\left(|\alpha_j|\left((1+\delta_1)\|\widehat{C}_j-\widetilde{C}_j\|+\|\widetilde{C}_j-C_j\|+\delta_1\|\widetilde{C}_j\|\right)\right).\text{(4.6)}\)

\(\left\|\widehat{C}-\sum_{j=1}^p\widehat{\alpha}_j\widehat{C}_j\right\|\le(\lceil log_2p\rceil+1)\left(\sum_{j=1}^p|\widehat{\alpha}_j|\|\widehat{C}_j\|\right)\mathbf{u}+O(\mathbf{u}^2),\) (4.7)

\(|\widehat{\alpha}_j|\|\widehat{C}_j\|\le(|\alpha_j|+|\widehat{\alpha}_j-\alpha_j|)\left(\|\widetilde{C}_j\|+\|\widehat{C}_j-\widetilde{C}_j\|\right)\le|\alpha_j|(1+\delta_1)\left(\|\widetilde{C}_j\|+\|\widehat{C}_j-\widetilde{C}_j\|\right).\) (4.8)

Combining (4.6) with (4.7) and (4.8) yields<tbc>

## 4.3 Parameter Selection for Improved Stability

Theorem 4.6 suggests that, from the point of view of stability, a good choice for the evaluation parameters \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\) is the _p_-th roots of unity - i.e., \(\varepsilon_j=e^{2\pi ij/p}\). In this case, the factor \(\prod_{i\neq j}\frac{|\varepsilon_i|}{|\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j|}\) simplifies to 1_/p_, and we do not have to worry about \(E(\varepsilon_j)\) blowing up due to large positive/negative powers of \(\varepsilon\) in the encoding matrices or basis transformations.

There is, however, one catch: the roots of unity, with the exception of \(\pm 1\) and \(\pm i\), are _not_ floating-point numbers, and hence Theorem 4.6 does not apply (in general) when \(\varepsilon_j=e^{2\pi ij/p}\). Instead, the best we can do is use the rounded roots of unity \(\tilde{\varepsilon}_1,\dots,\tilde{\varepsilon}_p\), which take the form \(\tilde{\varepsilon}_j=e^{2\pi ij/p}\cdot(1+\delta_j)\) for some \(|\delta_j|\le\mathbf{u}\). Importantly, for _p_ not too large, these approximate roots satisfy \(\prod_{i\neq j}\frac{|\tilde{\varepsilon}_i|}{|\tilde{\varepsilon}_i-\tilde{\varepsilon}_j|}=1/p+O(\mathbf{u})\). In particular, applying Theorem A.2 with \(\delta=\mathbf{u}\) and since the spacing between the _p_-th roots of unity is \(2\mathrm{sin}(\pi/p)\), we have the bound

\(\frac{|\tilde{\alpha}_j-1/p|}{1/p}\le\frac{(p-1)\mathbf{u}}{\mathrm{sin}(\pi/p)-p\mathbf{u}}\) (4.12)

for \(\tilde{\alpha}_1,\dots,\tilde{\alpha}_p\) the coefficients that solve the Vandermonde system corresponding to \(\tilde{\varepsilon}_1,\dots,\tilde{\varepsilon}_p\).

This implies the following corollary of Theorem 4.6, which assumes (1) that rounded roots of unity are used as evaluation points in Algorithm 4, and (2) that \(\tilde{\alpha}_1,\dots,\tilde{\alpha}_p\) and the entries of the encoding matrices/basis transformations at \(\tilde{\varepsilon}_1,\dots,\tilde{\varepsilon}_p\) are computed to high enough relative accuracy that \(g(\delta_1,\delta_2)\le 1+cp\mathbf{u}+O(\mathbf{u}^2)\) for some small constant _c\>_0. This specific bound is motivated by Theorem A.1.

## 5 Numerical Examples

In this section, we present a collection of numerical experiments aimed at verifying the theoretical results from the previous section. The first two explore the validity/tightness of our stability bounds (with and without alternative bases), while the third tests the effectiveness of the truncation idea discussed in Section 4.4. All experiments were done in Matlab and follow a common setup described in Section 5.1. Importantly, these experiments do not demonstrate the performance of APA matrix multiplication in a high-performance environment, which we leave to future work. Takeaways include the following:

1. Theorem 4.6 and Theorem 4.7, though not tight, effectively gauge the (relative) stability of APA routines.<tbc>

2. While alternative basis algorithms have a weaker stability bound, they perform no worse in practice.<tbc>

3. Truncation can significantly improve the run time of an APA matrix multiplication algorithm, trading mild accuracy loss for speed.

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

We implement several APA matrix multiplication routines, including some existing algorithms and some new ones found in our search. All implementations are recursive and run to the corresponding base case. That is, we do not default to classical or fast exact matrix multiplication at any point. Unless stated otherwise, we implement the full interpolation (i.e., Algorithm 4) using roots of unity to obtain an exact product (matching the setting of Theorem 4.7). In each experiment, we measure (relative) forward error via \(\|\widehat{C}-C\|/(\|A\|\|B\|)\), where \(\widehat{C}\) is the computed value of _C=AB_ and \(\|\cdot\|\) in the maximum-entry norm. Since we use random input matrices, each reported value of this error metric is the mean over ten independent draws of _A_ and _B_.

All algorithms for computing \(\widehat{C}\) are run in IEEE-754 binary64, whose corresponding unit roundoff is \(\mathbf{u}=2^{-53}\approx 1.11\times 10^{-16}\). To get a surrogate for the exact product _C=AB_, we convert _A_ and _B_ into symbolic form and evaluate the product in 32-digit arithmetic; relative error is then computed by evaluating \(\widehat{C}-C\) symbolically before rounding to double precision. All measurements were taken on an Apple M4 running macOS 26.5.1, with experiments performed in MATLAB version R2025b (25.2.0.3042426, Update 1) using the Symbolic Math Toolbox 25.2 and the Parallel Computing Toolbox 25.2.

## 6 Conclusion

This paper presented a deep dive into arbitrary precision approximate (APA) matrix multiplication. We provided both a new search algorithm for APA schemes and numerical analysis results aimed at understanding the practical performance of an APA algorithm. As mentioned in the introduction, the goal of this work was to renew interest in APA matrix multiplication, both from the theory and implementation perspectives.

In future work, we plan to pursue high-performance implementations of APA matrix multiplication algorithms with the goal of demonstrating results competitive with fast exact matrix multiplication (possibly in applications where lower precision is required). We have already identified several tools for accelerating APA algorithms - e.g., sparsification, truncation, etc. - but these have not yet been tested in a high- performance environment.
