## A Technical Results for Section 4

This appendix collects technical results used in the proof of our main stability bound (i.e., Theorem 4.6).

### A.1 Vandermonde Bounds

For a set of (distinct and nonzero) points \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\in\mathbb{C}\), consider the \(p\times p\) Vandermonde system

\(\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c c }
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\
\varepsilon_1 & \varepsilon_2 & \cdots & \varepsilon_p \\
\vdots & \vdots &  & \vdots \\
\varepsilon_1^{p-1} & \varepsilon_2^{p-1} & \cdots & \varepsilon_p^{p-1}
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ c }
\alpha_1 \\
\alpha_2 \\
\vdots \\
\alpha_p
\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{ c }
1 \\
0 \\
\vdots \\
0
\end{array}\right).\) (A.1)

Recall from Section 4 that the exact solution to this system is

\(\alpha_j=\prod_{k\neq j}\frac{\varepsilon_k}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j},1\le j\le p.\) (A.2)

Below, we derive the following:

1. A (relative) error bound for evaluating (A.2) in floating-point arithmetic (Theorem A.1).<tbc>

2. An (exact-arithmetic) perturbation bound for the \(\alpha_j\) (Theorem A.2).

We start with the floating-point error bound, which assumes the same model of floating-point arithmetic used in Section 4 (i.e, \[31, 48\]). Informally, Theorem A.1 implies that, under some mild assumptions, the \(\alpha_j\) can be computed accurately (in a relative sense) by simply evaluating (A.2) directly.

**Proposition A.1.** _Given distinct, nonzero_ \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\in\mathbb{C}\)_, let_

\(\alpha_j=\prod_{k\neq j}\frac{\varepsilon_k}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j}\text{\textit{for}}1\le j\le p.\)

_Suppose that the approximate quantities_ \(\widehat{\alpha}_1,\dots,\widehat{\alpha}_p\) _are the result of evaluating this expression in floating-point arithmetic, where we assume the following:_

1. _Each_ \(\varepsilon_i\) _is a normalized floating-point number._<tbc>

_2._ _The quotients_ \(\frac{\varepsilon_k}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j}\) _are evaluated directly and multiplied in an order that guarantees no over/underflow occurs._<tbc>

_3._ \(\frac{2(p-1)\mathbf{u}}{1-\mathbf{u}}<1\)_, where_ **u** _is the unit roundoff._<tbc>

<tbc>_In this case, we have_<tbc>

\(\frac{|\widehat{\alpha}_j-\alpha_j|}{|\alpha_j|}\le 3p\mathbf{u}+O(\mathbf{u}^2).\)

_Proof._ For fixed _j_, let \(y_k=\frac{\varepsilon_k}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j}\). If \(\widehat{y}_k\) is the value of this quantity in floating-point arithmetic, then<tbc>

\(\hat{y}_k=\frac{\varepsilon_k(1+\delta')}{(\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j)(1+\delta)}\text{for some}|\delta|,|\delta'|\le\mathbf{u}.\) (A.3)

<tbc>Equivalently, \(\widehat{y}_k=y_k\left(1+\mu_k\right)\) where \(|\mu_k|=\left|\frac{\delta'-\delta}{1+\delta}\right|\le\frac{2\mathbf{u}}{1-\mathbf{u}}\). Now \(\widehat{\alpha}_j\) is just a floating-point product of the \(\widehat{y}_k\). Assuming without loss of generality that this product can be computed from left to right without encountering over/underflow (the argument is the same for any ordering), the corresponding floating-point partial products \(\widehat{\Pi}_i\) satisfy

\(\widehat{\Pi}_1=\widehat{y}_1=y_1(1+\mu_1)\widehat{\Pi}_2=\widehat{y}_1\widehat{y}_2(1+\delta_1)=y_1y_2(1+\mu_1)(1+\mu_2)(1+\delta_1)\widehat{\Pi}_3=\widehat{\Pi}_2\widehat{y}_3(1+\delta_2)=y_1y_2y_3(1+\mu_1)(1+\mu_2)(1+\mu_3)(1+\delta_1)(1+\delta_2)\text{(A.4)}\)

\(\vdots\)

and therefore<tbc>

\(\widehat{\alpha}_j=\widehat{\Pi}_{p-1}=\alpha_j\cdot\prod_{k\neq j}(1+\mu_k)\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(1+\delta_k),\) (A.5)

<tbc>where each \(\delta_k\) satisfies \(|\delta_k|\le\mathbf{u}\). Since \(\frac{2(p-1)\mathbf{u}}{1-\mathbf{u}}<1\), standard bounds - e.g., \[31, Lemma 3.1\] - imply \(\prod_{k\neq j}(1+\mu_k)=1+\theta_1\) and \(\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(1+\delta_i)=1+\theta_2\) for

\(|\theta_1|\le 2p\mathbf{u}+O(\mathbf{u}^2)\text{and}|\theta_2|\le p\mathbf{u}+O(\mathbf{u}^2).\) (A.6)

Hence,

\(\frac{|\widehat{\alpha}_j-\alpha_j|}{|\alpha_j|}=|\theta_1+\theta_2+\theta_1\theta_2|\le|\theta_1|+|\theta_2|+|\theta_1||\theta_2|.\) (A.7)

The result now follows by applying (A.6).

We next prove a perturbation bound for (A.1).

**Proposition A.2.** _Let_ \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\in\mathbb{C}\) _be distinct and nonzero and define_<tbc>

\(gap_\varepsilon=min_{i\neq j}|\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j|\text{\textit{and}}M_\varepsilon=max_j|\varepsilon_j|.\)

<tbc>_Suppose that_ \(\tilde{\varepsilon}_1,\dots\) , \(\tilde{\varepsilon}_p\) _satisfy_<tbc>

\(\tilde{\varepsilon}_j=\varepsilon_j(1+\delta_j)\text{\textit{for}}|\delta_j|\le\delta,\)

<tbc>_where_ \(\delta>0\) _is the "size" of the relative perturbation. Let_ \((\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_p)\) _and_ \((\tilde{\alpha}_1,\dots,\tilde{\alpha}_p)\) _be the exact- arithmetic solutions to the Vandermonde system_ (A.1) _at the points_ \(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_p\) _and_ \(\tilde{\varepsilon}_1,\dots,\tilde{\varepsilon}_p\)_, respectively. If_ \(2(p-1)M_\varepsilon\delta<gap_\varepsilon-2M_\varepsilon\delta\)_, then_<tbc>

\(\frac{|\tilde{\alpha}_j-\alpha_j|}{|\alpha_j|}\le\frac{2(p-1)M_\varepsilon\delta}{gap_\varepsilon-2pM_\varepsilon\delta}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let \(y_k=\frac{\varepsilon_k}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j}\) and \(\tilde{y}_k=\frac{\tilde{\varepsilon}_k}{\tilde{\varepsilon}_k-\tilde{\varepsilon}_j}\). We have

\(\tilde{y}_k=\frac{\varepsilon_k(1+\delta_k)}{\varepsilon_k(1+\delta_k)-\varepsilon_j(1+\delta_j)}=\frac{\varepsilon_k}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j}\cdot\frac{1+\delta_k}{1+\frac{\varepsilon_k\delta_k-\varepsilon_j\delta_j}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j}}=y_k\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon_j(\delta_j-\delta_k)}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j+\varepsilon_k\delta_k-\varepsilon_j\delta_j}\right),\) (A.8)

where \(\mu_k=\frac{\varepsilon_j(\delta_j-\delta_k)}{\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_j+\varepsilon_k\delta_k-\varepsilon_j\delta_j}\) satisfies \(|\mu_k|\le\frac{2M_\varepsilon\delta}{gap_\varepsilon-2M_\varepsilon\delta}\). Hence,

\(\tilde{\alpha}_j=\prod_{k\neq j}\tilde{y}_k=\prod_{k\neq j}y_k(1+\mu_k)=\alpha_j\prod_{k\neq j}(1+\mu_k).\) (A.9)

Assuming \(\frac{2(p-1)M_\varepsilon\delta}{\mathrm{gap}_\varepsilon-2M_\varepsilon\delta}<1\) and again applying \[31, Lemma 3.1\], we can rewrite \(\prod_{k\neq j}(1+\mu_k)\) as follows:

\(\prod_{k\neq j}(1+\mu_k)=1+\theta\text{for}|\theta|\le\frac{2(p-1)M_\varepsilon\delta}{\mathrm{gap}_\varepsilon-2pM_\varepsilon\delta}.\) (A.10)

Inserting this above and rearranging yields the bound.

## A.2 Perturbation Bound for Bilinear Algorithms

Finally, we prove a perturbation bound for evaluating a recursive, alternative-basis bilinear algorithm in exact arithmetic.

**Proposition A.3.** _Let_ \(U_\phi\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0k_0\times t}\), \(V_\psi\in\mathbb{C}^{k_0n_0\times t}\), \(W_\nu\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0n_0\times t}\), \(\phi\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0k_0\times m_0k_0}\), \(\psi\in\mathbb{C}^{k_0n_0\times k_0n_0}\)_, and_ \(\nu^{-1}\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0n_0\times m_0n_0}\) _denote the encoding matrices and basis transformations defining an alternative basis bilinear map_<tbc>

\(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:\mathbb{C}^{m_0\times k_0}\times\mathbb{C}^{k_0\times n_0}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{m_0\times n_0}\)

<tbc>_evaluated as_<tbc>

\(c=\nu^{-1}\left[W_\nu\left(U_\phi^T(\phi^Ta)\odot V_\psi^T(\psi^Tb)\right)\right],\)

<tbc>_where a and b are vectorized copies of input matrices_ \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0\times k_0}\) _and_ \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k_0\times n_0}\) _and c is a vectorized copy of the corresponding output_ \(\langle A,B\rangle=C\in\mathbb{C}^{m_0\times n_0}\)_. Let_ \(C,\widetilde{C}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times n}\) _be the result of evaluating recursive versions of these bilinear algorithms at input matrices_ \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times k}\) _and_ \(B\in\mathbb{C}^{k\times n}\) _in exact arithmetic, where we assume that both default to matrix multiplication after L recursive steps for_ \(L\in\mathbb{N}\) _satisfying_<tbc>

\(L\le\mathrm{min}\left\{\mathrm{log}_{m_0}(m),\mathrm{log}_{n_0}(n),\mathrm{log}_{k_0}(k)\right\}.\)

<tbc>_In this case,_

\(\|C-\widetilde{C}\|\le\left((1+\delta)^{6L}-1\right)(k/k_0^L)E^L\|A\|\|B\|\)

_where_ \(\|\cdot\|\) _is the maximum-entry norm and E is the stability factor corresponding to_ \(U_\phi\), \(V_\psi\), \(W_\nu\), \(\phi\), \(\psi\)_, and_ \(\nu^{-1}\) _(see Theorem 4.3 )._

_Proof._ We prove the result via induction on _L_, starting with the inductive step. Assume that the given bound holds for _L_-1 and consider \(L\ge 2\). To evaluate our bilinear forms, we partition the input matrices into blocks as follows (assuming _m_<sub>0</sub>, _k_<sub>0</sub>, and _n_<sub>0</sub> divide _m_, _k_, and _n_):

\(A=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }

\vdots &  & \vdots \\
A_{m_01} & \cdots & A_{m_0k_0}

Each _A<sub>ij</sub>_ is \((m/m_0)\times(k/k_0)\) while each _B<sub>ij</sub>_ is (_k/k_<sub>0</sub>) by (_n/n_<sub>0</sub>). For this block partition, let a and b be _block_ vectorized copies of _A_ and _B_ - e.g.,
